docs.title: FortiGate Firewall – Block Social Media Websites (GUI)
FortiGate Firewall – Block Social Media Websites Using (GUI)
Overview
docs.text: FortiGate Web Filter allows network administrators to block access to specific websites like: www.youtube.com, www.facebook.com, www.instagram.com, domains, and URL paths.

docs.title: Configuration workflow
docs.text: Step 1         Create URL Filter Profile         Step 2         Apply Web Filter Profile         to Firewall Policy         Step 3         Test & Verify

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Web Filter Profile
docs.text:
1. Log in to the FortiGate GUI.

  2. Navigate to Security Profiles → Web Filter.

  3. Click Create New.

  4. Enter the profile name: Block-Social-Media.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Static URL Filter
docs.text:
Inside the new Web Filter profile:

  1. Find the Static URL Filter section.

  2. Enable URL Filter.

  3. Click Create New for each website.

  4. Add the following entries:

URL Type Action Status *youtube.com Wildcard Block Enable *facebook.com Wildcard Block Enable *instagram.com Wildcard Block Enable Purpose: Adds the social media websites to the URL block list.

Use the following example configuration: (Screenshot):

docs.title: Step 3: Apply the Profile to the Firewall Policy
docs.text:
A URL filter will not protect users unless the applicable traffic passes through a firewall policy with the Web Filter profile enabled.

  1. Go to Policy & Objects → Firewall Policy.

  2. Identify the policy that allows users to access the internet.

  3. Edit that policy.

  4. Enable Security Profiles or UTM Inspection, depending on the FortiOS version.

  5. Enable Web Filter.

  6. Select the profile Block-Social-Media.

  7. Enable SSL/SSH inspection as appropriate for your network.

  8. Save the policy.

Important: Edit the correct internet access policy. Do not change unrelated policies.

Use the following example configuration: (Screenshot):

docs.title: Step 4: Test the Configuration
docs.text:
1. Connect a client computer to the network.

  2. Open YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram.

  3. Confirm that the websites are blocked.

  4. If YouTube videos still play, check HTTPS inspection, QUIC/HTTP/3 traffic, and whether the correct firewall policy is being used.

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram should be blocked for users whose internet traffic passes through the configured firewall policy. Websites not matched by a blocking rule should remain accessible.

Note: GUI menu names can differ between FortiOS versions. Configuration must be tested on a client device to confirm that blocking is working.

docs.title: Check Web Filter logs
docs.text:
If the website is still accessible, check the logs:

  1. Navigate to Log & Report → Security Events.

  2. Open the Web Filter events.

  3. Filter for the client's source IP address or the destination hostname.

  4. Review the action, matched URL, profile, and policy ID.

  5. Look for an entry with an action such as blocked and a message indicating that the URL matched the local URL filter.

Use the following example configuration: (Screenshot):

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: FortiGate firewalls also allow administrators to block Web Filter feature and firewall policies using graphical user interface (GUI) as well as Command Line Interface (CLI).

docs.title: Step 1: Create the URL Filter Table
docs.text:
1. Log in to the FortiGate firewall using SSH, a console connection, or the CLI Console available in the web interface.

  2. First, create a URL filter table and add a rule to block social media sites.

config webfilter urlfilter
    edit 1
        set name "Social-Media-URLs"
        config entries
            edit 1
                set url "*youtube.com"
                set type wildcard
                set action block
            next
            edit 2
                set url "*facebook.com"
                set type wildcard
                set action block
            next
            edit 3
                set url "*instagram.com"
                set type wildcard
                set action block
            next
        end
    next
end

Purpose: Creates a URL Filter table containing the websites to be blocked.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure the Web Filter Profile
docs.text:
config webfilter profile
    edit "Block-Social-Media"
        config web
            set urlfilter-table 1
        end
    next
end

Purpose: Links URL Filter table ID 1 to the Block-Social-Media profile.

docs.title: Step 3: Apply the Profile to the Firewall Policy
docs.text:
First, identify the firewall policy used for internet access:

show firewall policy

Use the actual policy ID in the following commands. The example below uses policy ID 1.

config firewall policy
    edit 1
        set utm-status enable
        set webfilter-profile "Block-Social-Media"
    next
end

Purpose: Enables security inspection and applies the custom Web Filter profile to the selected firewall policy.

Important: Modify the correct internet access policy to avoid affecting other network traffic.

docs.title: Step 4: Verify the Configuration
docs.text:
Check the URL Filter table

show webfilter urlfilter

Check the Web Filter profile

show webfilter profile "Block-Social-Media"

Check the firewall policy

show firewall policy

Confirm that the correct policy has the following settings

set utm-status enable
set webfilter-profile "Block-Social-Media"

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
• YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram should be blocked for users whose traffic passes through the configured firewall policy.

  • The custom Web Filter profile should be applied to the correct policy.

  • Test the websites from a client computer to confirm that blocking works.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If YouTube videos still play after applying the configuration, check HTTPS inspection, QUIC/HTTP/3 traffic, and whether the traffic is actually passing through the configured policy.

Note: Configuration alone does not guarantee successful blocking. Always test and verify the result on the client device.

docs.title: Important Consideration:
docs.text:
1. Correct Policy ID: Verify that you are modifying the correct LAN-to-WAN firewall policy handling the client's traffic.

  2. Profile Association: Ensure the Static URL Filter list is linked to the intended Web Filter profile and that the profile is applied to the relevant firewall policies.

  3. Wildcard Matching: Configure URL patterns carefully, such as *facebook.com, because matching behavior may vary with the pattern and FortiOS version.

  4. HTTPS Inspection: URL filtering capabilities depend on the SSL inspection profile and the visibility available for encrypted traffic.

  5. Additional Domains: Applications may use additional domains, content delivery networks (CDNs), and alternate endpoints. Blocking one domain may not block the entire application.

  6. QUIC and HTTP/3: These protocols can affect filtering behavior. Review QUIC handling if blocking is incomplete.

  7. Existing Configuration: Review existing firewall and security profiles before making changes to avoid overwriting required settings.

  8. FortiOS Compatibility: Confirm command syntax and supported features for your FortiGate FortiOS version.

  9. Production Deployment: Test changes in a controlled environment before applying them to production networks.

Official Reference: Fortinet's FortiOS 7.4.8 Administration Guide. Your interface may differ slightly. Reference Source: Fortinet — Static URL Filter and verification

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Blocking a website on FortiGate using CLI involves three main tasks: configuring a Static URL Filter, associating it with a Web Filter profile, and applying that profile to the appropriate firewall policy.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To establish a formal procedure for the daily management, maintenance, and operational integrity of the Property Management System (PMS), ensuring seamless Front Office operations, system availability, and accurate guest data management.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This SOP applies to all members of the IT Department responsible for administering, monitoring, securing, maintaining, and troubleshooting the Property Management System (PMS) and its integrated systems.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
• Execution: IT Manager and IT Executive.

  • Monitoring: IT Manager.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Perform a daily system health check of the PMS server, connected terminals, and associated services.

  2. Verify the successful completion of the nightly audit and scheduled data backups.

  3. Review system logs for errors, warnings, unusual activities, and unauthorized access attempts.

  4. Monitor PMS integrations, including the Point of Sale (POS), key card system, and Private Branch Exchange (PBX), to confirm that all interfaces are online and communicating correctly.

  5. Create, modify, and deactivate PMS user accounts according to approved requests and employee roles.

  6. Verify that appropriate access permissions are assigned to authorized personnel based on their job responsibilities.

  7. Coordinate with the Front Office and Reservations teams to investigate and resolve PMS-related issues promptly.

  8. Record all PMS incidents, troubleshooting activities, and corrective actions in the IT ticketing system.

  9. Apply approved software patches and updates during off-peak hours, following vendor recommendations and change management procedures.

  10. Verify system functionality after maintenance or updates and confirm that critical PMS services are operating normally.

  11. Escalate major incidents, recurring errors, and potential data integrity issues to the IT Manager and relevant stakeholders.

  12. Maintain daily health check reports, access records, maintenance logs, and backup verification records.

docs.title: Standards & Guidelines
docs.text:
• PMS access must be granted according to the principle of least privilege and business requirements.

  • Routine maintenance should be scheduled during low-occupancy or off-peak periods to minimize operational disruption.

  • The target PMS system availability should be 99.9% or higher, subject to approved service requirements and vendor capabilities.

  • All PMS-related incidents, service requests, and changes must be documented in the IT ticketing system.

  • Software updates and configuration changes must be authorized and performed according to approved change management procedures.

  • User accounts must be reviewed periodically, and access must be revoked promptly when no longer required.

  • Data backups must be monitored regularly, and restoration procedures should be tested according to the hotel's backup policy.

  • Any suspected security incident or guest data exposure must be reported immediately through the hotel's incident escalation process.

docs.title: Records & Documentation
docs.text:
The following records must be maintained:

  • Daily PMS system health check reports.

  • IT ticketing system logs for PMS-related incidents and service requests.

  • PMS user access records and change logs.

  • Nightly audit verification reports.

  • Data backup completion and verification reports.

  • Software update and maintenance records.

  • PMS incident investigation and resolution reports.

  • System availability and downtime records.

docs.title: Safety & Precautions
docs.text:
• Never share, disclose, or reuse PMS login credentials in an unauthorized manner.

  • Use strong passwords and approved authentication controls wherever supported.

  • Handle guest information with strict confidentiality and in accordance with applicable data protection requirements and hotel policies.

  • Do not make unauthorized changes to PMS configurations, user permissions, or integrated systems.

  • Verify backup completion before performing maintenance that could affect system data or availability.

  • Maintenance requiring system downtime must be communicated in advance and approved by the General Manager and relevant Department Heads.

  • Follow the hotel's incident response and escalation procedures in the event of system failure, suspected unauthorized access, or data loss.

  • Ensure that critical PMS functions are verified after maintenance before returning the system to normal operation.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text: To protect the resort’s network and computing infrastructure from malware, viruses, and unauthorized data transfers through effective antivirus protection and USB device management.

docs.title: 2. Scope
docs.text: This SOP applies to all IT Department personnel and covers all resort-owned computing devices, including servers, desktops, laptops, and Point of Sale (POS) terminals.

docs.title: 3. Responsibility
docs.text:
• Execution: IT Executive

  • Monitoring and Compliance: IT Manager

docs.title: 4.1 Antivirus Management
docs.text:
1. Ensure that approved antivirus software is installed and active on all resort-owned computing devices.

  2. Update antivirus definitions automatically wherever possible, or perform manual updates when required.

  3. Perform weekly full system scans on all mission-critical servers and desktops.

  4. Monitor the centralized antivirus management console for security alerts, detected threats, quarantined files, and scan status.

  5. Investigate and remediate detected threats according to the resort’s IT security procedures.

  6. Immediately isolate any device suspected of being infected to prevent the spread of malware across the network.

docs.title: 4.2 USB Device Management
docs.text:
1. Disable USB autorun functionality on all applicable resort-owned computing devices.

  2. Permit only IT-approved, scanned, and whitelisted USB storage devices.

  3. Scan every USB storage device using approved antivirus software before accessing or transferring files.

  4. Prohibit the use of personal or unauthorized USB storage devices on resort computers.

  5. Maintain an official whitelist of approved USB devices, including device identification details and authorization status.

  6. Remove or revoke authorization for USB devices that are lost, compromised, or no longer required.

docs.title: 5. Standards & Guidelines
docs.text:
• Antivirus definitions must be updated at least once every 24 hours.

  • Antivirus protection must remain enabled and operational on all supported devices.

  • Weekly full system scans must be completed and documented for mission-critical servers and desktops.

  • Devices with detected or suspected malware must be isolated from the network immediately, following established incident response procedures.

  • Personal and unauthorized USB storage devices must not be connected to resort-owned computers.

  • Only authorized and whitelisted USB devices may be used for business purposes.

  • The IT Department must maintain an up-to-date USB device whitelist.

  • Any antivirus failure, suspicious activity, or security incident must be reported promptly to the IT Manager.

docs.title: 6. Records & Documentation
docs.text:
The IT Department must maintain the following records:

  • Centralized antivirus console reports, including detected threats, quarantined files, and scan history.

  • Antivirus definition update logs and records of manual updates.

  • Full system scan logs and remediation records.

  • Approved USB device whitelist and authorization records.

  • Security incident reports and corrective actions taken.

docs.title: 7. Safety & Precautions
docs.text:
1. In the event of a suspected malware outbreak, immediately isolate affected devices from the network to prevent lateral spread.

  2. Do not delete quarantined files or disable antivirus protection without proper authorization.

  3. Do not connect unknown, personal, or unapproved USB storage devices to resort-owned computers.

  4. Report serious security incidents immediately to the IT Manager and General Manager.

  5. Preserve relevant security logs and evidence for investigation, where applicable.

docs.title: 8. Compliance
docs.text: All IT personnel must follow this SOP. Any exception to antivirus or USB security controls requires prior authorization from the IT Manager and must be documented.

docs.title: Connecting the Dots: 5 Essential Network Types Shaping Our Digital World
docs.text: Whether checking a smartwatch, jumping onto an office Wi-Fi network, or syncing data across continents, digital communication feels completely effortless. Behind this seamless user experience lies a carefully engineered hierarchy of network architectures, each tailored for specific distances, bandwidth demands, and security requirements. In this article, we break down the five core network architectures that power our connected world.

docs.title: 1. Personal Area Network (PAN): The Ultra-Local Bubble Around You
docs.text:
The Personal Area Network (PAN) is the smallest geographic network type, operating directly around an individual to connect hardware like smartphones and wearables. These ultra-local environments rely on specialized short-range technologies, specifically Bluetooth, ZigBee, and USB interconnects. By handling immediate data exchange without heavy infrastructure, PANs serve as the essential foundation for modern wearable technology and mobile device integration.

As defined in core networking specifications:

"A short-range network used for personal devices... using Bluetooth, ZigBee, or USB interconnects."

docs.title: 2. Local Area Network (LAN): High-Speed Powerhouse of the Workplace
docs.text: Step into any modern office or single building, and you enter the domain of the Local Area Network (LAN). A LAN provides high-speed data transmission across a localized physical footprint using established technical standards: Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) for wired reliability and Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) for wireless coverage. Because a single organization typically maintains administrative control over a LAN, engineers can finely tune network parameters, eliminating external bottlenecks to deliver high throughput and dedicated local bandwidth.

docs.title: 3. Metropolitan Area Network (MAN): Bridging the Campus and City Gap
docs.text: Scaling upward to cover municipal spaces, a Metropolitan Area Network (MAN) spans an entire city or a consolidated enterprise or educational campus. These regional backbones are primarily owned and operated by Internet Service Providers (ISPs) or large enterprise entities. To move high volumes of traffic across city-sized distances, MANs leverage robust transmission technologies, including Ethernet MAN, DWDM (Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing), and microwave transmission. A MAN acts as a crucial intermediate backbone, connecting separate local sites across a city without demanding full global infrastructure.

docs.title: 4. Wide Area Network (WAN): The Global Interconnect
docs.text:
Crossing regional borders and oceans, Wide Area Networks (WANs) handle communication over immense physical distances. A WAN functions as a sprawling infrastructure designed to interconnect disparate LANs across counties, countries, or continents. It achieves this global reach through dedicated leased lines—such as MPLS (Multi-Protocol Label Switching) and Metro Ethernet—or via public networks, like the Internet paired with VPN tunneling. Because WAN traffic regularly traverses public spaces, robust security mechanisms such as IPSec or SSL/TLS are critical to safeguarding sensitive data across vast distances.

As highlighted in industry technical references:

"A geographically distributed network that interconnects LANs over large distances..."

docs.title: 5. Virtual Private Network (VPN): The Secure Overlay on Public Roads
docs.text: Unlike the physical network topographies described above, a Virtual Private Network (VPN) functions as a secure overlay network built directly on top of existing public infrastructure, typically the Internet. Instead of laying dedicated physical wires to grant private network access across long distances, a VPN constructs encrypted tunnels using protocols like IPSec and SSL-VPN. Transforming open public infrastructure into private, encrypted pathways allows organizations to provide secure remote access to users connecting from anywhere in the world.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: From short-range PANs and localized LANs to city-wide MANs, global WANs, and secure VPN overlays, these five network types operate as an integrated ecosystem to maintain continuous digital flow. Together, they ensure data moves safely and efficiently whether syncing a wearable, collaborating in an office, or connecting across continents. Which of these network architectures do you rely on most throughout your average day?

docs.title: The Invisible Blueprint: Decoding the Network Topologies That Power Our Digital World
1. Introduction: The Invisible Blueprint of Digital Communication
docs.text:
Every day, millions of connected devices quietly exchange vast amounts of data across the globe. Yet, despite our constant reliance on this seamless connectivity, we rarely pause to consider the structural blueprints that dictate how information actually moves from point A to point B.

Behind every digital interaction lies a network topology—the physical or logical arrangement of computers, network devices, and communication links within a network. In simple terms, network topology describes how devices are connected to each other and how data travels between them.

Understanding these underlying blueprints reveals the fundamental mechanics of modern connectivity—how raw hardware layouts and logical data pathways intersect to forge the invisible infrastructure supporting our digital age.

docs.title: 2. Takeaway 1: What You See Isn't Always How Data Flows (Physical vs. Logical Topology)
docs.text:
To evaluate network design effectively, one must recognize that every network possesses two distinct identities: its physical topology and its logical topology. For network builders, distinguishing between these two domains is essential for constructing reliable, maintainable systems.

Physical topology refers to the actual physical arrangement of network devices, cables, ports, and other hardware components. It answers the practical question of how equipment is physically wired and positioned in space. In contrast, logical topology defines how devices communicate and how data travels through the network, regardless of physical appearance or cable routes.

"Logical topology refers to how data flows between devices across a network, regardless of the physical arrangement of the devices and cables."

docs.title: 3. Takeaway 2: The Redundancy Spectrum—Trading Simplicity for Reliability
docs.text:
Designing a network requires navigating fundamental engineering trade-offs. Architects must continually weigh capital expenditure and implementation complexity against the imperative for systemic fault tolerance. Topologies exist along a structural spectrum, ranging from simple, cost-effective layouts to highly redundant architectures built for continuous operation.

At the high-reliability extreme sits the Mesh topology. By equipping devices with multiple interconnections—and in a full mesh configuration, connecting every device directly to every other device—it provides exceptional redundancy and reliability. This robust architecture makes it the blueprint of choice for redundant WAN connections, even though its financial cost and implementation complexity remain high.

As reliability requirements shift or budgetary constraints intervene, architects step down the redundancy spectrum toward simpler compromise models. Star topology offers an easily managed framework ideal for localized office LANs, while Bus topology minimizes cabling requirements by linking devices along a single path, as seen in older Ethernet networks.

Topology Type Primary Advantage Main Risk or Drawback Star Easy to manage and troubleshoot Central device failure impacts entire network Bus Uses less cable Backbone failure disrupts the entire network Mesh High redundancy and reliability Expensive and complex to implement

docs.title: 4. Takeaway 3: The Danger of the Single Point of Failure
docs.text:
In non-redundant network topologies, localized structural flaws can expose the entire system to complete collapse. Without built-in failovers, a single localized fault triggers a cascade of failure across the network:

  • Star Topology: Centralized dependency defines this layout, where every device connects directly to a central switch or hub. While this centralization makes the network easy to manage and troubleshoot, a failure of that central device immediately isolates all endpoints and impacts the entire network.
  • Bus Topology: Shared medium vulnerabilities govern this architecture, as all devices share a single main backbone cable. Because every transmission relies on this common pathway, a single physical break or failure in the backbone cable disrupts the entire network.
  • Ring Topology: Sequential routing dictates data movement in this arrangement, where each device connects to two neighboring devices to form a continuous loop. Utilized in legacy ring networks, this sequential path means that a single link failure can disrupt a basic, unprotected ring.

docs.title: 5. Takeaway 4: How Modern Enterprises Scale (Tree and Hybrid Topologies)
docs.text:
As organizations expand, simple point-to-point or single-hub structures rapidly hit scaling bottlenecks. Real-world enterprise environments resolve these growth challenges by implementing hierarchical and mixed structures.

Tree topology organizes devices into a hierarchical structure complete with branching paths. Frequently deployed across an enterprise campus network, this model makes expanding and organizing large numbers of endpoints straightforward. However, it retains top-down structural dependencies: the failure of an upper-level device can compromise all of its subordinate branches.

To achieve superior operational resilience, organizations frequently deploy a Hybrid topology, combining two or more distinct topology types. A classic enterprise implementation combines local star LANs with a redundant backbone network. While hybrid and tree topologies increase design and troubleshooting complexity, they deliver the flexibility and scalability required to support modern enterprise operations.

docs.title: 6. Conclusion: Choosing the Right Network Blueprint
docs.text:
Every network topology represents a set of strategic trade-offs between cost, structural complexity, ease of management, and fault tolerance. No single blueprint is universally superior; rather, the optimal network architecture depends entirely on the operational requirements, budget, and reliability demands of the system.

As you navigate your daily digital interactions, consider this: what kind of topology powers the invisible connections in your own office or daily digital life?

docs.title: Everything You Need to Know About Computer Networks and Why They Power Our Digital World
1. Introduction: The Invisible Web Connecting Our Daily Tech
docs.text: When you log onto your office Wi-Fi to send a document to a shared printer or transfer a critical file to a teammate, you are relying on an invisible web of modern technology. But what actually happens behind the scenes when our everyday devices communicate with one another? This guide breaks down the fundamental elements and immense value of computer networks in simple, accessible terms.

docs.title: 2. Key Takeaway 1: A Network Is More Than Just Computers—It's an Ecosystem
docs.text:
At its foundational level, a computer network is a group of components or other devices connected together to communicate, exchange data, and share resources such as files, printers, applications, and an internet connection. Rather than functioning as a collection of isolated machines, a network operates as a synchronized ecosystem composed of distinct hardware categories:

  • End Devices: Computers, servers, printers, and smartphones.
  • Network Devices: Hub, Modem, Switch, Router, Repeater, Network Interface Card (NIC), Bridge, Wi-Fi Access Point, and Firewall.

Understanding this hardware diversity matters because modern networking depends on a seamless balance between user-facing endpoints and background infrastructure. For instance, when end devices like workstations and printers interact, they rely directly on network hardware like a Wi-Fi Access Point to bridge the digital gap:

"Computers connected to the same Wi-Fi network in an office can share files and access a common printer."

docs.title: 3. Key Takeaway 2: The Core Purpose Is Resource and Cost Efficiency
docs.text:
The rapid adoption of computer networks across enterprise environments was not merely a technological trend—it was driven by fundamental economic and practical necessity. Connecting devices yields two central capital and operational advantages: 1. Easy Sharing of Files & Information: Facilitating immediate, frictionless data transfer across all connected hardware to accelerate organizational workflows. 2. Hardware Optimization: Allowing multiple endpoints to share high-cost, high-value assets—specifically dedicated Servers and Printers—rather than forcing organizations to deploy duplicate units for every individual user.

By maximizing capital efficiency and eliminating duplicate infrastructure costs, resource sharing transformed enterprise IT budgets and established computer networking as the indispensable operational backbone for modern offices.

docs.title: 4. Key Takeaway 3: Physical Paths and Invisible Protocols Make It Work
docs.text:
For data to travel successfully across a network, two complementary enabling layers must operate in tandem: physical pathways that move bits, and logical standards that interpret them.

  • Transmission Media (The Highways): The physical and wireless conduits used to transport raw data from point to point, specifically Ethernet cables, fiber-optic cables, and Wireless connections.
  • Protocols (The Language Rules): The governing set of standardized communication rules that dictate how hardware interprets and structures data, including TCP/IP, HTTP, FTP, DNS, SMTP, and Telnet.

While transmission media provide the essential physical or wireless pathways required for data movement, protocols establish the logical rules of engagement. Without standardized protocols like TCP/IP or HTTP acting as a universal translator, raw signals moving across cables or airwaves would remain indecipherable to receiving devices.

docs.title: 5. Conclusion: The Backbone of Modern Connectivity
docs.text: By unifying end devices, specialized network hardware, transmission media, and standardized protocols into a single cohesive system, computer networks make everyday data exchange effortless. Together, these underlying components form the invisible architecture that drives global digital connectivity. As you finish reading this, take a moment to reflect: how many distinct network devices and protocols did you rely on just to load this single article online?
